issues.legal_issue: A prompt first information report need not contain every detail of an occurrence, and an eyewitness account that is substantially consistent with it may be accepted despite a discrepancy about an inferred detail.
material_facts: An eyewitness gave the first information report within two hours of the incident while agitated and emotionally disturbed.
At trial, the eyewitness said the victim was not hit by the pistol shot and fell as bundles of wheat fell on him; the medical evidence disclosed no firearm injury.
The eyewitness consistently described the other accused as inflicting injuries, and her account was supported by the statement of an injured witness and the medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no material contradiction between the report and the eyewitness's testimony and upheld reliance on both; the alleged discrepancy did not make the eyewitness untrustworthy.
issues.legal_principle: A first information report is not substantive evidence; it is relevant in assessing the veracity of the prosecution case, and its value depends on the circumstances. It need state only the essential or broad picture, need not catalogue every act or serve as an encyclopaedia of the occurrence, and omissions or vague references are not necessarily fatal. The Court relied on Ram Kumar v. State of M.P. (AIR 1975 SC 126), Bishan Das v. State of Punjab (AIR 1975 SC 573), Podda Narayana v. State of A.P. (AIR 1975 SC 1252), Gurnam Kaur v. Bakshish Singh (AIR 1981 SC 631), State of Haryana v. Sher Singh (AIR 1981 SC 1021), State of U.P. v. Ballabh Das (AIR 1985 SC 1384), Joginder Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1988 SC 628), and Baldev Singh v. State of Punjab (1990 (4) SCC 692).

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and prompt_report_by_distressed_witness and eyewitness_account_substantially_matches_report and discrepancy_concerns_inferred_detail

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The accused pursued an appeal from convictions arising out of a criminal trial.
predicates.prompt_report_by_distressed_witness: A distressed eyewitness gave the initial report soon after the occurrence.
predicates.eyewitness_account_substantially_matches: The eyewitness's account at trial substantially matched the account in the initial report.
predicates.discrepancy_concerns_inferred_detail: The alleged inconsistency concerned a detail the witness had inferred rather than a material difference in the account of the occurrence.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a criminal conviction and a distressed eyewitness promptly gives a substantially consistent account, a discrepancy about an inferred detail does not by itself discredit that account.

issues.legal_issue: Where the accused caused injuries resulting in death but the evidence and circumstances did not establish murder, the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
material_facts: The accused were close family members, and the incident arose from a dispute over cultivation and family property.
The Court accepted that two accused caused injuries to one victim and that one accused alone caused injuries to the other victim.

The injuries attributed to the appellants were on the thigh and back; the medical evidence disclosed no firearm wound, and no evidence or finding identified who caused the fatal injuries to the first victim.
The Court considered the weapons and circumstances insufficient to establish an intention to cause death or knowledge that death was likely from the injuries inflicted.
The second victim died about eight days after the incident, and the injuries inflicted on him were not proved to be serious or fatal.
issues.conclusion: The Court altered the murder convictions to convictions for culpable homicide under Section 299 read with Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 299, 300, 302 and 304 of the Indian Penal Code and the three-stage analysis in State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (1977 (1) SCR 601): determine whether the accused caused the death, whether the act amounts to culpable homicide under Section 299, and whether the case falls within Section 300. The Court concluded on these facts that the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under Section 304, Part I.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_caused_death_resulting_injuries and fatal_injury_attribution_unproved and injuries_confined_to_nonvital_parts and circumstances_do_not_establish_murder_intent_or_knowledge

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The accused appealed convictions for murder arising from a criminal proceeding.
predicates.accused_caused_death_resulting_injuries: The accused caused injuries that resulted in a victim's death.
predicates.fatal_injury_attribution_unproved: The evidence did not establish which accused caused the fatal injury or injuries.
predicates.injuries_confined_to_nonvital_parts: The injuries attributed to the accused were confined to parts of the body not shown to be vital.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_establish_murder_in: The weapons, injuries, and surrounding circumstances did not establish an intention to cause death or knowledge that death was likely.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a murder conviction and caused death-resulting injuries, but the fatal injury is unattributed, the injuries were confined to nonvital parts, and the circumstances do not establish the required murder intent or knowledge, the conviction is for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

issues.legal_issue: A court may limit imprisonment to the custody already undergone and order compensation for victims or their families when the circumstances make compensation an appropriate response to the offence.
material_facts: The victims and the accused were near relations, and a family property dispute led to the incident.
The deceased victim's widow and children suffered an irreparable loss, and the Court considered that imprisonment alone would not benefit them.
The appellants were in a position to pay compensation and had already served more than two years in custody before being released on bail.
The Court directed that compensation be paid to the widow and children and provided for recovery and revival of the trial-court sentence if it was not paid.
issues.conclusion: The Court limited the appellants' imprisonment to the period already undergone and ordered each appellant to pay compensation to the deceased victim's widow and children, with the trial-court sentence to revive if the compensation was not paid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 357(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits compensation to be ordered in addition to other sentences. In deciding whether and how much compensation is appropriate, the court should consider the nature of the crime, the injury suffered, the justness of the claim, the offender's capacity to pay, and other relevant circumstances. The Court referred to Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh (1988 (4) SCC 551), Dr. Jacob George v. State (1994 (3) SCC 430), and Balraj v. State of U.P. (1994 (4) SCC 29).

rule.if: criminal_sentencing_appeal and victim_family_suffered_serious_loss and offender_has_capacity_to_pay and imprisonment_alone_will_not_benefit_victims and compensation_is_just_in_the_circumstances

predicates.criminal_sentencing_appeal: The accused appealed the sentence imposed in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.victim_family_suffered_serious_loss: The victim's family suffered serious loss as a result of the offence.
predicates.offender_has_capacity_to_pay: The offender was in a position to pay compensation.
predicates.imprisonment_alone_will_not_benefit_vict: The court considered that imprisonment alone would not benefit the victims or their family.
predicates.compensation_is_just_in_the_circumstance: The nature of the offence, the injury suffered, and the surrounding circumstances made compensation appropriate.

issues.definition: When a sentencing appeal shows serious loss to the victim's family, capacity to pay, and circumstances in which imprisonment alone will not benefit the victims, imprisonment may be limited to custody already undergone and compensation ordered.

issues.legal_issue: The conviction and sentence for possessing a weapon without a licence could be set aside in the appeal.
material_facts: The trial court convicted one appellant under the Arms Act for possessing a barchha without a licence.
The appellants appealed the convictions and sentences, and the Supreme Court set aside the Arms Act conviction and sentence.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the conviction and sentence under the Arms Act.
issues.legal_principle: The Court's operative order set aside the Arms Act conviction and sentence, but the judgment does not state a separate reason or legal analysis for doing so.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The accused pursued an appeal from convictions arising out of a criminal trial.
predicates.arms_act_conviction_for_unlicensed_weapo: The appeal included a conviction for possessing a weapon without a licence under the arms law.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction appeal includes a conviction for unlicensed weapon possession under the arms law, the ruling in this case sets that conviction and its sentence aside.
